explanation: Kot is a masculine consonant-ending noun. Its nominative singular is the dictionary form, with no added ending; compare feminine książka and neuter dziecko.
Książka is a feminine noun whose dictionary form ends in -a. The nominative singular keeps that -a, unlike masculine kot or neuter dziecko.
Dziecko is neuter and its nominative singular ends in -o. Here the naming form is unchanged; the plural dzieci must be learned separately.
Student is masculine personal. Its nominative plural studenci has a changed stem and -i; contrast feminine książki and irregular neuter dzieci.
Kot is masculine animate, a group that commonly has genitive singular -a: kota. Inanimate czas instead has lexical -u: czasu.
Feminine książka changes final -a to -i after k, giving książki. Compare szkoła → szkoły, which takes -y after ł.
Masculine inanimate czas has genitive singular czasu with -u. Masculine genitive -a versus -u is partly lexical: learn this noun's form rather than applying one ending to all masculine nouns.
Feminine książka has genitive plural książek: no added plural case ending, but e appears in the stem. Compare masculine kotów and irregular neuter dzieci.
This masculine animate noun uses the shorter dative singular -u: kotu. Another masculine noun, przyjaciel, uses -owi: przyjacielowi.
Przyjaciel is masculine personal and takes common dative singular -owi. Kot → kotu shows that masculine nouns do not all choose the same dative ending.
Feminine kobieta takes -e/-ie in dative singular and the stem softens: t → ci, giving kobiecie. Compare neuter dziecko → dziecku.
Dative plural commonly uses -om. Dziecko first has the irregular plural stem dzieci-, giving dzieciom; compare kotom and książkom.
Kot is masculine animate. Its accusative singular matches its genitive singular, kota; inanimate dom instead stays dom.
Dom is masculine inanimate, so its accusative singular matches the nominative dom. Masculine animate kot instead uses kota.
Feminine książka ends in -a, which commonly becomes -ę in accusative singular: książkę. Neuter dziecko remains dziecko.
Student is masculine personal. Its accusative plural matches genitive plural studentów; animal kot has non-masculine-personal plural koty instead.
Masculine kot takes common instrumental singular -em: kotem. Feminine książka takes -ą instead: książką.
Feminine -a noun książka replaces -a with -ą in instrumental singular: książką. Contrast masculine kotem.
Neuter dziecko has instrumental singular dzieckiem. The written i before -em keeps the sound after k; compare kotem without i.
Dziecko has irregular instrumental plural dziećmi with -mi and a changed stem. The common plural ending is -ami, as in kotami.
Kot uses locative singular -ie with stem softening t → c: kocie. Dom instead has locative domu with -u.
Dom has lexical locative singular -u: domu. Kot uses -ie and a changed stem: kocie. Learn which pattern each noun follows.
Feminine książka uses -e with k → c in locative singular: książce. Some feminine nouns use -y/-i instead, such as praca → pracy.
Locative plural commonly takes -ach. Dziecko has the irregular plural form dzieciach rather than a simple dziecko + ending; compare kotach and książkach.
When addressing a cat, kot has vocative singular kocie with t → c and -ie. Other masculine nouns may take -u, such as przyjacielu.
Feminine mama changes final -a to -o in vocative singular: mamo. Familiar names can differ, such as Kasia → Kasiu.
Masculine przyjaciel uses vocative singular -u: przyjacielu. Kot instead has -ie with a softened stem: kocie.
Plural vocative normally matches nominative plural. For masculine-personal student, that form is studenci, with a changed stem and -i.
